minor.issue: It says all 87 athletes provided 7-day iPhone screen-time data ('objectively recorded'). In fact 7 participants (8%) self-reported or were assumed to have self-reported use.
The source text shows Clin J Sport Med 2021;00:1-7. The 2022;32(5):486-492 details cannot be verified from the text.
It does not say that the analyses were ANCOVA controlling for romantic relationship status and binary logistic regression, that groups were tertile-based, or that team-sport athletes were excluded.
It does not mention the small, mostly female sample, the unmeasured sleep duration, or that the PROMIS t-score (52.1) stayed in the none-to-slight range, which limits clinical relevance.
It does not note that 7 participants self-reported social media use instead of providing iPhone data.
'mostly female' slightly overstates a 54% female sample, though the authors themselves describe a 'predominance of female participants'.

note: Both records are accurate. B adds the PROMIS 52.1 versus cut-off 55 context, the borderline Facebook P=0.049, the total-time aOR 1.002 (P=0.103) and the analytic details, all of which the source supports.
